--- title: "1.5 Assignments" ---
![](../../src/images/hex_complex.png){.intro_image} We have used assignments in our previous lessons, but I have held back on the urge to explain or describe how and why to manage them. In this lesson, we will take a deeper dive into the assignment process. You will learn: * What global assignments are (mostly review) * Assignment in recursive objects * Naming conventions for assignments * The pros and cons of nested and non-nested function calls * How to avoid global assignments with the pipe operator * How to manage global assignments with `rm()` ::: {.callout-important} This lesson assumes that you have completed the preliminary lessons. As the material covered herein will build on the content in those lessons, please do not proceed until their completion. :::
## Setup Please create a new script file, save it as `scripts/1.5_assignments.R`, and run the following line to attach the core tidyverse packages: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) ``` ::: Before starting this activity, please visit "Global Options/Code" and ensure that the checkbox "Use native pipe operator ..." is **not checked**. ## Global assignments Recall that when we **assign** (verb) an object to a name, R typically creates a binding between the name and object in the global environment. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nerdy_greeting <- "hello world" ``` ::: We can use `ls()` to generate and print a character vector of assignments in the global environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ls() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "nerdy_greeting" ``` ::: ::: *Note: If my goal for an operation is only to print some output, I typically complete the operation in the console pane.* The name provides us with a means to retrieve the object from the global environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nerdy_greeting ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "hello world" ``` ::: ::: Remember, however, that the name is stored in our global environment, but the values themselves are stored in our computer's memory. We can view this explicitly using the function `ref` from the *lobstr* package: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lobstr::ref(nerdy_greeting) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `loadNamespace()`: ! there is no package called 'lobstr' ``` ::: ::: The above shows the address of the object in our computer's memory (yours will be different than mine) and the class of the object (``). If we run `lobstr::ref()` and specify the target object as the global environment (with `.GlobalEnv`), we can get a glimpse of how the data are stored: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lobstr::ref(.GlobalEnv) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `loadNamespace()`: ! there is no package called 'lobstr' ``` ::: ::: The above shows a **reference tree produced by lobstr**. This visualization displays object addresses and relationships among objects. Here, the global environment (``) is an object stored in memory at a specified address. The global environment contains a binding from the name `nerdy_greeting` to the character vector in memory. Because evaluating a name retrieves the object associated with that name, the object itself and the name associated with that object can often be used interchangeably. Let's create another one-value character vector and assign it to the name `southern_saying`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} southern_saying <- "boy howdy!" ``` ::: We can use the *stringr* (core tidyverse) function `str_c()` to paste together strings with some separator (`sep = ...`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_c( nerdy_greeting, southern_saying, sep = ", " ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "hello world, boy howdy!" ``` ::: ::: Notice in the above that R evaluated each name to retrieve the associated character vector. Because of this, the following expressions all yield equivalent results: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_c( "hello world", "boy howdy!", sep = ", " ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "hello world, boy howdy!" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} str_c( nerdy_greeting, "boy howdy!", sep = ", " ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "hello world, boy howdy!" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} str_c( "hello world", southern_saying, sep = ", " ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "hello world, boy howdy!" ``` ::: ::: The power of this process for generating easy-to-write and human-readable code becomes readily apparent with increased complexity. Let's generate a numeric vector and extract the third value in the set with the extraction function (`[[...]]`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(0, 1, 1, 2)[[3]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: The above works, but is definitely hard to read. Let's assign the vector `c(0, 1, 1, 2)` to the name `fibo_numbers`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fibo_numbers <- c(0, 1, 1, 2) ``` ::: ... and reference the name to extract the third value from the set: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fibo_numbers[[3]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: We can see that assigning the object to a name makes life much easier! In both instances, R stores the vector in memory. With `c(0, 1, 1, 2)[[3]]`, the output of `c(0, 1, 1, 2)` is passed to the `[[...]]` function and becomes eligible for garbage collection after the expression is evaluated. With the assignment version, the numeric vector `c(0, 1, 1, 2)` is stored in memory, we reference the vector by supplying the name `fibo_numbers`, and again extract the data by index with `[[...]]`. ::: mysecret {{< fa screwdriver-wrench size=2x >}} [Assign "a name to an object" or "an object to a name"?]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} We often informally say "assign `name` to `object x`." Recall from ***Preliminary Lesson 2: Environment & Functions***, however, that a single object can have multiple names. As such, the correct way to describe this is "assign `object x` to `name`." To explore this further (and perhaps start to see *why* this matters), let's assign the object retrieved with `nerdy_greeting` to the name `temp`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} temp <- nerdy_greeting ``` ::: ... and have another look at the reference tree of the global environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lobstr::ref(.GlobalEnv) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `loadNamespace()`: ! there is no package called 'lobstr' ``` ::: ::: In the above, we can see that, although they have different names, the addresses of `temp` and `nerdy_greeting` in memory are the same! This illustrates why "names have objects" rather than "objects have names". ::: ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} After running `temp <- nerdy_greeting`, which statement is correct?
::: ### Removing names Assignment is very useful, and assigning objects to names is a necessary skill, but it is important to recognize that the number of assigned names can impact your computer's performance during an R session. Especially as data get big (as they tend to do in ecology), having your computer store a bunch of data objects in its memory is really inefficient. Because of this (and a few other reasons), I *strongly* recommend managing your global environment with care! In practice, that means that you should: * Limit the number of assigned names; * Remove assigned names when they are no longer needed. We'll address the first bullet point later in this lesson (the Pipe Operator). For now, we'll focus our attention on the second bullet point -- removing assigned names. Let's start by adding a few more names to our global environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ordered_numbers <- 1:20 musicians <- c( "roger", "pete", "john", "keith" ) four_instruments <- c( "vocals", "guitar", "bass", "drums" ) ls() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "fibo_numbers" "four_instruments" "musicians" "nerdy_greeting" [5] "ordered_numbers" "southern_saying" "temp" ``` ::: ::: #### Single names We can remove a name assigned to the global environment with the remove function, `rm()`. We call the function by supplying its name (`rm`), followed by parentheses, and then the name that we would like to remove from the global environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rm(temp) ls() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "fibo_numbers" "four_instruments" "musicians" "nerdy_greeting" [5] "ordered_numbers" "southern_saying" ``` ::: ::: Notice what happens when we type `temp` now: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} temp ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error: ! object 'temp' not found ``` ::: ::: Because we removed the name, R cannot retrieve the object through `temp`. If no other reference remains, the object becomes eligible for garbage collection. ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [What about `rm("temp")`?]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} An area of confusion among many students is when quotes are, and are not, necessary. Quotes are not necessary when: * Referencing a name assigned to your global environment; * The name when assigning an object to a name (e.g., `name <- "hello world"`). Because `temp` was a name assigned to the global environment, the quotes are not necessary. As such, `rm("temp")` should be written more parsimoniously as `rm(temp)`. The exception occurs when a given name breaks R's variable-naming rules (e.g., `1howdy`). ::: #### Multiple names If we want to remove multiple names from our global environment, we use `rm()` and separate each name with a comma: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rm(ordered_numbers, fibo_numbers) ``` ::: If we want to remove *all* of the assignments in our global environment, we need to supply a new argument to `rm()`. Have a look at the help file for the function (`?rm`). Note that: * In the *Usage* section of the help file, we can see that the second argument of the function is `list = character()`. * In the *Arguments* section of the help file, we see that the input for that argument is "a character vector (or NULL) naming objects to be removed". You might have noticed that the `ls()` function returned a character vector of names assigned to our global environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ls() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "four_instruments" "musicians" "nerdy_greeting" "southern_saying" ``` ::: ::: The above can be verified with the `class()` function, which will tell us the class of the resultant object: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class( ls() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: Because `ls()` returns a character vector where each value is a name assigned to the global environment, we can remove all the assignments with: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rm( list = ls() ) ls() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` character(0) ``` ::: ::: ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Use `rm()` from within your script file!]{style="padding-left: 1em; font-size: 1.25em;"} Removing a name from your global environment can have downstream effects (i.e., impacts code run later in a script). If `rm()` removes a name that was assigned to your global environment in your script file, avoid conducting this operation in the console pane. ::: ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} True or false: `rm(list = ls())` removes every name returned by `ls()` from the global environment. ::: ## Recursive assignments Recall that **recursive objects** are objects that are made up of references to other objects. Examples include lists and data frames (which, of course, *are* lists). Let's generate a list that contains the character values `nerdy_greeting` and `southern_saying` and assign the list to the name `my_list`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list <- list("hello world", "boy howdy!") my_list ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [[1]] [1] "hello world" [[2]] [1] "boy howdy!" ``` ::: ::: Our list currently does not have a `names` attribute. `lobstr::ref()` shows the list and the objects associated with its elements: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lobstr::ref(my_list) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `loadNamespace()`: ! there is no package called 'lobstr' ``` ::: ::: Notice that the structure of a list is quite different from the vectors it contains. This can become even more apparent by combining the values into a character vector rather than a list and observing how the data are stored: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_sayings <- c("hello world", "boy howdy!") lobstr::ref(my_sayings) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `loadNamespace()`: ! there is no package called 'lobstr' ``` ::: ::: `lobstr::ref()` shows a single object address for the atomic vector. For the list, it shows the list's address and the addresses of the objects associated with its elements. Because a list is a recursive object, we can name its elements using `=` within `list()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list_named <- list( nerdy_greeting = "hello world", southern_saying = "boy howdy!" ) lobstr::ref(my_list_named) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `loadNamespace()`: ! there is no package called 'lobstr' ``` ::: ::: The above works because a list can have a name associated with each of its elements. In these lessons, I will call names within a data object (list or data frame) **recursive assignments**. This is my own terminology for names stored in the object's `names` attribute. These names are distinct from bindings in an environment. We can generate and print a character vector of the recursive assignments themselves using the primitive `names()` function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} names(my_list_named) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "nerdy_greeting" "southern_saying" ``` ::: ::: Recursive assignments do not directly live within the global environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nerdy_greeting ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error: ! object 'nerdy_greeting' not found ``` ::: ::: To access the data associated with the assignment, we need to call the child object from within the parent object. We can extract data from a list object by name using the extraction operator `[[...]]`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list_named[["southern_saying"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "boy howdy!" ``` ::: ::: The above works because the character index matches the list element's name. We can also use the extraction operator `$` to extract a named list element: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list_named$southern_saying ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "boy howdy!" ``` ::: ::: We can add an assignment to a list (or data frame!) by assigning a new name and associating that name with some data: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list_named$salutations <- c("good day", "fare thee well") lobstr::ref(my_list_named) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `loadNamespace()`: ! there is no package called 'lobstr' ``` ::: ::: We can change the data associated with a name by assigning the name to a different data object: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list_named$salutations <- factor(my_list_named$salutations) lobstr::ref(my_list_named) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `loadNamespace()`: ! there is no package called 'lobstr' ``` ::: ::: Similarly, we can remove a recursive name, and in fact in the entire list element, by assigning the value `NULL` to the name: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list_named$salutations <- NULL lobstr::ref(my_list_named) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `loadNamespace()`: ! there is no package called 'lobstr' ``` ::: ::: ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Can I use `$` for named atomic vectors? No!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} Students have often asked me why they cannot use `$` for atomic vectors. Notice what happens if we try to name the values in an atomic vector: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_sayings_named <- c( nerdy_greeting = "hello world", southern_saying = "boy howdy!" ) lobstr::ref(my_sayings_named) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `loadNamespace()`: ! there is no package called 'lobstr' ``` ::: ::: The values can still have names, but `$` is only defined for recursive objects and environments. The following therefore returns an error: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_sayings_named$southern_saying ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `my_sayings_named$southern_saying`: ! $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors ``` ::: ::: Use `my_sayings_named[["southern_saying"]]` to extract the named element instead. ::: ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} Which expression extracts the element named `southern_saying` from `my_list_named`?
::: ## Naming conventions A consistent naming convention, both for names in the global environment and recursive names, will save you time and make your code and output more readable. Let's read in the file `badNameDataFrame.csv`, assign the object to the name `bad_df` and print the data to see what the data frame looks like: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bad_df <- read_csv("data/raw/badNameDataFrame.csv") bad_df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 BED LightAccess `plant/mushroom` `Event date` gardenEvent 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: We can see that the naming convention in this object is *all over the place*. In working with these data, you are going to struggle to remember the naming convention used for each variable when referencing the columns. Remembering column names is hard enough! Modern R coding conventions suggest using the "snake_case" naming convention for all names (global and recursive assignments). With the **snake_case** naming convention all letters are lowercase and all words are separated with an underscore (`_`). We can see in the printout above that two of the variables, `plant/mushroom` and `Event date`, are surrounded by backticks. That is because they are **non-syntactic variable names**, which are invalid variable names (e.g., names that start with a number or include unusual characters). Neither the symbol `/` nor spaces are allowed in variable names. To make it possible to reference these variables, all non-syntactic variable names are surrounded by backticks. Notice that attempting to use a non-syntactic variable name without backticks produces a warning message and an error: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} unique(bad_df$plant/mushroom) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error: ! object 'mushroom' not found ``` ::: ::: We have to continue to use backticks whenever we reference the column: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} unique(bad_df$`plant/mushroom`) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA "lion's mane" "oyster mushrooms" "shitake" [5] "mesclun" "jalapenos" "tomatoes" "edamame" [9] "kale" "summer squash" "corn" "acorn squash" ``` ::: ::: Clearly it is in our best interest to rename these variables! ### Rename with `rename()` One option for renaming variables is the *dplyr* (core tidyverse package) function `rename()`. We supply the name of the data frame and then, after a comma, `new_variable_name = old_variable_name`. For example, let's change `BED` to lowercase `bed`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rename(bad_df, bed = BED) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed LightAccess `plant/mushroom` `Event date` gardenEvent 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: The variable `LightAccess` is in **PascalCase** (also called UpperCamelCase), a naming convention in which the first letter of each word is capitalized. We can change multiple names by separating additional `new_variable_name = old_variable_name` with a comma: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rename( bad_df, bed = BED, light_access = LightAccess ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access `plant/mushroom` `Event date` gardenEvent 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: To rename our non-syntactic variable names, we need to ensure that we include the backticks when referencing them: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rename( bad_df, bed = BED, light_access = LightAccess, plant_mushroom = `plant/mushroom`, event_date = `Event date` ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access plant_mushroom event_date gardenEvent 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: Our last problem column is in **camelCase**, a naming convention in which the first word is not capitalized and the first letter of subsequent words *are* capitalized. Before the snake_case naming convention rose to prominence, camelCase was the preferred convention in R. Let's change `gardenEvent` to snake_case: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rename( bad_df, bed = BED, light_access = LightAccess, plant_mushroom = `plant/mushroom`, event_date = `Event date`, garden_event = gardenEvent ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access plant_mushroom event_date garden_event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} Reorder the lines below to assign a version of `bad_df` in which `BED` and `LightAccess` have snake_case names. One line supplies the arguments in the wrong order. Leave it in the trash.

::: ### `set_names()` The `rename()` function is great but only works for data frame objects ... it does not work for lists or atomic vectors! The `set_names()` function is a part of the *rlang* package and made available with `library(tidyverse)` through the *purrr* package (part of the core tidyverse). We can use `set_names()` to assign names to an object. We supply the object that we would like to assign names to and an atomic character vector of names: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list_add_names <- set_names( my_list, c("Nerdy", "Southern") ) my_list_add_names ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $Nerdy [1] "hello world" $Southern [1] "boy howdy!" ``` ::: ::: Notice in the above that I did not follow our snake_case naming convention. To change this, we can refer to the original names assigned to the object and convert those names to lowercase with base R's `tolower()` function. I will show this in a single step and then break it down: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set_names( my_list_add_names, tolower( names(my_list_add_names) ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $nerdy [1] "hello world" $southern [1] "boy howdy!" ``` ::: ::: The above worked because `names()` generates a character vector of names: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} names(my_list_add_names) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Nerdy" "Southern" ``` ::: ::: ... and `tolower()` converts a character vector to lowercase: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tolower( names(my_list_add_names) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "nerdy" "southern" ``` ::: ::: ## Nested and non-nested function calls You may have noticed that the above was a little hard to read. As we covered in ***Preliminary Lesson 2: Environment & Functions***, it is what is known as a "nested function call." A **nested function call** occurs when the output of one function is passed directly to another function. Let's look again at our nested operation above: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set_names( my_list_add_names, tolower( names(my_list_add_names) ) ) ``` ::: This describes a **chained analysis**, an operation in which the output of one function is used as the input of another. Reviewing the operation again, the chained analysis was evaluated in the following order: 1. The `names()` function generated a character vector of names in `my_list_add_names`. 2. The `tolower()` function converted the character vector above to lowercase and returned a character vector. 3. The `set_names()` function converted `my_list_add_names` (the first argument in the function) based on the character vector of names supplied in step 2. Because nested function calls are evaluated from the innermost call to the outermost call, they are very hard to read. **I do not recommend nesting function calls more than two layers deep** (and have only done so above for illustration purposes). An alternative to nesting functions is to make your code more legible by using assignments. It might look something like: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} original_names <- names(my_list_add_names) lowercase_names <- tolower(original_names) set_names(my_list_add_names, lowercase_names) ``` ::: The above is certainly more human-readable, but can lead to a lot of names unnecessarily clogging up your global environment. If we use these assignments again, we will have to remember what we called them, which can be challenging and lead to a lot of backtracking through your code (thus a time-consuming and messy workflow). If we are not going to use the assignments again, it is considered best practice to remove them: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rm(original_names, lowercase_names) ``` ::: Once we get to real data, it will be clear that processes like this might improve code readability, but at a big expense to your R script length and workflow. *Note: You can also reduce names in your global environment by reusing them, but you should typically avoid overwriting assigned objects.* As a review of the strengths and weaknesses of the two approaches: **Nested code**: * Strengths: Concise and no new names to manage; * Weaknesses: It can be difficult to read at even modest levels of complexity. **Non-nested code using assignments**: * Strength: Easy to read. * Weaknesses: It takes up a lot of script space and includes assignments that require additional management. ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} In which order does R evaluate the nested expression that renames `my_list_add_names` with lowercase names?
::: ## The pipe operator An alternative to hard-to-read nested code and hard-to-manage non-nested code with assignments is the pipe operator. A pipe operator is an infix function that passes the data object on the left-hand side (LHS) to the function on the right-hand side (RHS). In these lessons, we will use the `%>%` pipe operator, which is in the *magrittr* package and made available to us with `library(tidyverse)` (*Note: magrittr is not, however, a package in the core tidyverse*). To see how a pipe operator works, let's return to the non-nested assignment version of our list-naming process: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} original_names <- names(my_list_add_names) lowercase_names <- tolower(original_names) set_names(my_list_add_names, lowercase_names) ``` ::: Our first operation was to extract a character vector of names from `my_list_add_names`. By default, the pipe operator passes the LHS object to the first argument of the RHS function. This could therefore be written as: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list_add_names %>% names() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Nerdy" "Southern" ``` ::: ::: *Note: The pipe operator can, and should, be inserted using the keyboard shortcut Ctrl + Shift + M (Windows) or Command + Shift + M (Mac).* The above produced a character vector of names. We can continue the chain, using the character vector returned by `names()` as the object input (LHS) of `tolower()` (RHS): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list_add_names %>% names() %>% tolower() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "nerdy" "southern" ``` ::: ::: Note that this is operationally equivalent to the nested version of the code: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tolower( names(my_list_add_names) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "nerdy" "southern" ``` ::: ::: The difference is that the steps in the chained analysis are written in the same order as they are executed. That makes piped code *way* easier to read! For our last step, we have a choice to make. Notice that the vector of new names is the second argument of `set_names()` (see `?set_names`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set_names(my_list_add_names, lowercase_names) ``` ::: *Note: I did not run the above because we have removed `lowercase_names` from the global environment.* Because the end of our chained operation is a character vector of names, we *could* nest that operation inside of `set_names()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set_names( my_list_add_names, my_list_add_names %>% names() %>% tolower() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $nerdy [1] "hello world" $southern [1] "boy howdy!" ``` ::: ::: This is a reasonably easy to read operation because, though the code is nested, it is still only nested two levels deep. Another option is to use a **placeholder symbol** -- in the context of piping, this defines the location in the RHS function where the data will be piped into. The placeholder for the *magrittr* pipe is a period: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list_add_names %>% names() %>% tolower() %>% set_names(my_list_add_names, .) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $nerdy [1] "hello world" $southern [1] "boy howdy!" ``` ::: ::: The above works because the pipe passed the data to the location of the period. At this level of simplicity, either method is acceptable (but my preference is the placeholder method). As our data puzzles become more complex throughout these lessons, we will find opportunities to use both. ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [But doesn't base R have its own pipe?]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} Base R released its own pipe operator in 2021 (R release 4.1.0) -- the `|>` symbol. As of this writing, there are still a couple of tricks that I regularly use with *magrittr's* pipe that cannot be replicated with the base R pipe. As such, I have decided to use `%>%` throughout these lessons. ::: ### Reduce assignments with pipes Let's consider our reading and re-naming operation with the tabular dataset "data/raw/badNameDataFrame.csv". Previously, we read in the file, assigned the object, and then renamed the columns (not evaluated): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bad_df <- read_csv("data/raw/badNameDataFrame.csv") rename( bad_df, bed = BED, light_access = LightAccess, plant_mushroom = `plant/mushroom`, event_date = `Event date`, garden_event = gardenEvent ) ``` ::: Chances are, we will *never* use the version of `bad_df` with the non-standard column names after renaming them. Notice that the first argument of `rename()` is the target data frame. As such, the above could be rewritten as: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_csv("data/raw/badNameDataFrame.csv") %>% rename( bed = BED, light_access = LightAccess, plant_mushroom = `plant/mushroom`, event_date = `Event date`, garden_event = gardenEvent ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access plant_mushroom event_date garden_event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: Notice that the first argument was left blank because `%>%` inserted the left-hand-side result as the first argument of `rename()`. This piped version is equivalent to a nested version of the code (not evaluated): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rename( read_csv("data/raw/badNameDataFrame.csv"), bed = BED, light_access = LightAccess, plant_mushroom = `plant/mushroom`, event_date = `Event date`, garden_event = gardenEvent ) ``` ::: Although the above is not too deeply nested, I prefer the piped version because it allows us to focus our attention on only the renaming process. Before moving on, let's bring `set_names()` back into the picture. Notice that we have changed *all* of the names in our data frame. The `rename()` function is great for changing one or two names -- when changing all of the names, `set_names()` is my preference because we can simply provide a vector of new names. Written with the assignment version, this might look like (not evaluated): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_df <- read_csv("data/raw/badNameDataFrame.csv") set_names( my_df, c( "bed", "light_access", "plant_mushroom", "event_date", "garden_event" ) ) ``` ::: With the nested version of the process, this would be written as: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set_names( read_csv("data/raw/badNameDataFrame.csv"), c( "bed", "light_access", "plant_mushroom", "event_date", "garden_event" ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access plant_mushroom event_date garden_event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: ... of course, because the data frame is the first argument of `set_names()`, the operation could be written more simply using piping with: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_csv("data/raw/badNameDataFrame.csv") %>% set_names( c( "bed", "light_access", "plant_mushroom", "event_date", "garden_event" ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access plant_mushroom event_date garden_event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: #### Reducing assignments with the placeholder method The placeholder method, when used with Magrittr's pipe, can offer a lot of flexibility in how we code. For example, perhaps we want to subset the garden to beds that are in full sun. Without pipes (or placeholders), this is a multistep process. First we'll read in the data and repair the names: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} garden_names_repaired <- read_csv("data/raw/badNameDataFrame.csv") %>% set_names( c( "bed", "light_access", "plant_mushroom", "event_date", "garden_event" ) ) ``` ::: And then use the extraction operator `[]` to subset the data to just garden beds that are classified as "full sun" (see ***Preliminary Lesson 5: Indexing***): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} garden_sunny <- garden_names_repaired[garden_names_repaired$light_access == "full sun", ] ``` ::: Notice, however, that the left-hand-side (LHS) arguments of the extraction functions above, `[]` and `$`, are the data that you wish to subset. As such, you can use the placeholder (`.`) to pipe the data into these positions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Read in the data: read_csv("data/raw/badNameDataFrame.csv") %>% # Change the variable naming convention: set_names( c( "bed", "light_access", "plant_mushroom", "event_date", "garden_event" ) ) %>% .[.$light_access == "full sun", ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 27 × 5 bed light_access plant_mushroom event_date garden_event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 1 full sun jalapenos 2020-04-12 planted 8 2 full sun tomatoes 2020-04-14 planted 9 6 full sun edamame 2020-04-15 planted 10 4 full sun summer squash 2020-04-17 planted # ℹ 17 more rows ``` ::: ::: We can take this a step further. Perhaps we want to generate a character vector of unique plants in our full sun beds. We can continue with the above with: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Read in the data: read_csv("data/raw/badNameDataFrame.csv") %>% # Change the variable naming convention: set_names( c( "bed", "light_access", "plant_mushroom", "event_date", "garden_event" ) ) %>% .[.$light_access == "full sun", ] %>% # Subset to the variable plant_mushroom: .$plant_mushroom %>% # Subset the character vector to unique values: unique() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA "jalapenos" "tomatoes" "edamame" [5] "summer squash" "corn" "acorn squash" ``` ::: ::: ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [To assign or not to assign?]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} *Almost* all of my code contains global assignments, but I do not assign objects very often. Some rules to help you: * If you only use an assigned name once or twice, opt for a pipe operator instead * If the assignment represents a data object that took a long time to process (on the computer end), use an assignment * If the assignment represents a data object that took a ton of code to create, and *not* assigning the object would require that code to be replicated, use an assignment ::: ### Piping around your code Piped code can be readily explored! In this video, I demonstrate a process that I call "piping around your code": {{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/ZIeL0lp83rY?si=bnKZgXlk5_Dl04X7 >}} ## Exercises ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Test your knowledge!]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} 1. One line reverses the arguments supplied to `set_names()`. Leave it in the trash.

::: ## Take-home points * Assignment creates or changes a binding between a name and an object. A single object may be retrieved through more than one name. * Use `rm()` to remove names that are no longer needed, and make those changes from the script when they affect later code. * Lists and data frames can contain named elements. Extract those elements with `[[...]]` or `$`, and assign `NULL` to remove an element. * Use a consistent snake_case naming convention. Use `rename()` to change selected data-frame variables and `set_names()` when supplying a complete vector of names. * Pipes express a chained analysis in the order in which it runs. They can reduce temporary assignments while keeping code readable. ## Reference ::: panel - **Placeholder symbol**: In the context of piping, the symbol that defines the location in the right-hand-side function where the piped data will be inserted (a period, `.`, for the *magrittr* pipe). - **Recursive assignments**: Names within a data object (a list or data frame), as opposed to names within the global environment. - **Recursive object**: An object made up of references to other, nested objects (e.g., a list). - **Snake_case**: A naming convention in which all letters are lowercase and words are separated with an underscore (`_`). ::: ::: panel **Important!** Primitive functions, as well as functions in the packages that R attaches by default (e.g., *base*, *utils*, *stats*, and *graphics*), are available as soon as you start an R session. ::: function_table ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
